title: Per-State Signatures and Mean Time-to-Failure: An Algorithm for Systems With Simultaneous Failures

paper.title: Per-State Signatures and Mean Time-to-Failure: An Algorithm for Systems With Simultaneous Failures
paper.abstract:
Abstract We present an algorithm that computes the structural signature and the mean time-to-failure (MTTF) of a monotone binary system at every one of its states, rather than only at the state in which all components work.
It makes no assumption on the structure function and evaluates it exactly once per state, as many times as needed for the signature of the complete system alone, so computing the MTTF everywhere costs only a factor polynomial in the number of components over computing it once.
As a by-product, it identifies all minimal path sets.
We assume exchangeable component failure times whose survivor count is a continuous-time Markov chain.
This setting admits simultaneous failures, as in the Lévy-frailty Marshall-Olkin, binomial failure rate and lethal-shock models, where the simplifications available for single failures do not apply.
We use the per-state MTTF to define threshold repair policies.
We show that the per-state signature is a strictly finer decision criterion than the MTTF: signature dominance at a common failure count implies MTTF dominance, but not conversely.
Under the Lévy-frailty Marshall-Olkin model the MTTF is monotone in the state, which yields the long-run cost rate of every threshold policy in a single pass.
Experiments on 22 benchmark networks with up to 30 components and 31 failure models show that the best MTTF-threshold policy has a median excess cost of 0.36% over the optimal state-based policy, and that it is never worse than the best policy that repairs after a fixed number of failures.

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: Reliability indices of a multi-component system are almost always reported for the system with every component working. Maintenance decisions, however, are taken at partially failed states: an operator observes which components have failed, and must decide whether to keep operating or to intervene. Two states with the same number of failed components can differ sharply in how much useful life remains, depending on which components failed, and a decision rule that ignores this distinction discards information that is available for free. Acting on it requires the reliability index not at one state, but at all of them. In this work we provide an algorithm that computes the structural signature and the mean time-to-failure (MTTF) at each of the 2 n 2^{n} states of a monotone binary system with n n components, at essentially the cost of computing them once.

sections.heading: I-B Computational challenge due to the exponential number of states
sections.text: Although 𝐬 \mathbf{s} and 𝐒 ¯ \bar{\mathbf{S}} have only n n entries, obtaining them demands, in principle, the status Φ ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) \Phi(\mathbf{x}) at all 2 n 2^{n} states. For a system with n = 30 n=30 components this means 2 30 2^{30} bits, or 128 128 megabytes, merely to store the system status; for n = 40 n=40 it means 128 128 gigabytes. Moreover, a single entry can already dominate the count: for n = 40 n=40 , computing S ¯ ⌊ n / 2 ⌋ \bar{S}_{\lfloor n/2\rfloor} requires determining how many of the ( 40 20 ) = 137,846,528,820 \binom{40}{20}=137{,}846{,}528{,}820 states with 20 20 failed components still work. The difficulty is intrinsic rather than an artifact of this formulation, since exact reliability evaluation is # ​ P \#\mathrm{P} -complete already for networks [ 9 ] . Computing the signature at every state is, at first sight, considerably worse. The subsystem induced by a state 𝐱 \mathbf{x} —the system restricted to the components working in 𝐱 \mathbf{x} — has its own signature, so one would need 2 n 2^{n} signature vectors: ( n 0 ) \binom{n}{0} of dimension n n , ( n 1 ) \binom{n}{1} of dimension n − 1 n-1 , and so on. Naively, each of them costs a full enumeration of that subsystem’s own states.

sections.heading: I-C Contributions
sections.text: We show that this pessimism is unwarranted, and that the per-state signatures and MTTFs come at a modest premium over the single-state computation. Specifically: 1. We give a recursion (Lemma 1 ) that obtains the counting vectors of a state from those of its immediate sub-states, and an algorithm (Algorithm 1 ) that sweeps the state space by levels of failure count. Theorem 2 shows that the algorithm evaluates the structure function exactly 2 n 2^{n} times —the same number required to compute the signature of the complete system alone— and that computing the MTTF at all states, instead of at one, costs only a polynomial factor in n n in memory and in basic arithmetic operations. No assumption whatsoever is made on Φ \Phi . 2. We work under exchangeable failure times whose survivor-count process is a continuous-time Markov chain. This admits simultaneous failures of several components, as caused by common-cause shocks, and it is exactly the regime in which the simplifications available for single failures break down. We delimit the resulting model class precisely, and illustrate it with several families of failure models, including the Lévy-frailty Marshall-Olkin family and the binomial failure rate and lethal-shock models of probabilistic safety assessment. 3. As a corollary, the same sweep identifies all minimal path sets of the system, at no additional cost in evaluations of Φ \Phi . 4. We use the per-state MTTF to define threshold repair policies, and compare them through their long-run expected cost rate. We further show (Theorem 5 ) that signature dominance at a common failure count implies MTTF dominance, and that the MTTF is a single linear projection of the per-state signature; consequently, signature-threshold policies strictly refine MTTF-threshold policies. Under the Lévy-frailty Marshall-Olkin distribution the MTTF is monotone in the state (Lemma 4 ), and we show that this yields the long-run cost of all MTTF-threshold policies in a single pass over the states, grouped into classes with the same counting vector (Proposition 3 ). All costs include a setup cost per repair intervention. We also compute the optimal state-based policy, which bounds what any policy based on the per-state signature can achieve. 5. We report computational experiments on 22 benchmark networks with up to 30 components, 31 failure models calibrated to a common pairwise beta factor, and 45 cost settings (Section VII ). The best MTTF-threshold policy has a median excess cost of 0.36 % 0.36\% over the optimal state-based policy, and it is never worse than the best r r -out-of- n n policy, over which it saves a median of 4.2 % 4.2\% ; its cost curve, however, is neither convex nor unimodal in the threshold, i.e., it can increase and then decrease again, so the threshold must be tuned over all breakpoints.

sections.heading: I-D Organization
sections.text: Section II reviews related work. Section III states our assumptions on the failure-time distribution and formulates the per-state MTTF. Section IV presents the recursion, the algorithm and its complexity analysis. Section V develops the MTTF-threshold repair policies and their long-run cost, and the optimal state-based policy. Section VI establishes the dominance and expressiveness results. Section VII reports the computational experiments, and Section VIII concludes. The proofs of all results are in Appendix A .

sections.heading: Signatures and their computation
sections.text: Since its introduction by Samaniego [ 1 ] , the signature has become a standard tool for comparing and evaluating coherent systems [ 2 , 3 ] : stochastic orders between systems follow from orders between their signatures [ 10 ] , and the decomposition ( 4 ) extends from iid to exchangeable lifetimes [ 8 ] , the setting we adopt. Marichal et al. [ 7 ] gave the counting form ( 2 ), and Coolen and Coolen-Maturi [ 6 ] the survival signature for several component types. Computing the signature exactly is the practical bottleneck. Existing methods enumerate minimal path or cut sets [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] , or use symbolic representations of the structure function such as binary decision diagrams [ 14 ] , and they target the signature of the complete system. We need one signature per state, i.e., 2 n 2^{n} of them, and we are not aware of an algorithm that produces these, for an arbitrary structure function, at a cost comparable to a single signature computation.

sections.heading: Reliability of used and partially failed systems
sections.text: Mixture representations of the residual lifetime of a used system [ 15 ] , and of its conditional residual life given the number of failures and the system status [ 16 ] , condition on the number of failed components rather than on their identity. They are representations rather than algorithms: obtaining the value at every state from them would repeat the derivation state by state, without exploiting that neighboring states share almost all of their sub-states, which is what Lemma 1 does.

sections.heading: Exchangeable models with a Markov survivor count
sections.text: Ross, Shahshahani and Weiss [ 17 ] identified the structure on which Assumptions (A)–(B) of Section III rest; the model of Ross [ 18 ] , in its exchangeable case, and sequential order statistics with exponential baseline [ 19 ] are single-failure instances. Together, (A) and (B) force a pure-death chain on the number of working components, which excludes models based on Markovian arrival processes [ 20 , 21 ] , semi-Markov multi-state models [ 22 ] and exchangeable dependent-renewal constructions [ 23 ] ; among the models they admit, the Lévy-frailty Marshall-Olkin family is the richest tractable one with simultaneous failures.

sections.heading: Simultaneous and common-cause failures
sections.text: The multivariate exponential distribution of Marshall and Olkin [ 24 ] is the canonical model of common shocks; its specializations in probabilistic safety assessment are the binomial failure rate [ 25 , 26 ] and lethal-shock [ 26 ] models. The Lévy-frailty Marshall-Olkin family [ 27 ] is its exchangeable subclass driven by a Lévy subordinator, whose order statistics and asymptotics were analyzed in [ 28 , 29 ] , and repair policies and decompositions in [ 30 ] . We note in Section VII-A that the binomial failure rate and lethal-shock models are of Lévy-frailty type, so this family covers the standard common-cause models.

sections.heading: Maintenance driven by reliability indices and by signatures
sections.text: Signature-based maintenance is surveyed in [ 31 ] . Finkelstein et al. [ 32 ] proposed “time-free” policies triggered by the number of failed components; in these and related policies the trigger is a scalar index, and the signature enters only through the expected costs and cycle lengths. Closest to our setting, Feng and Yun [ 33 ] replace all failed components once the mean residual life of the system drops below a tuned threshold; Section V discusses why their computation is not viable beyond very small systems.

sections.heading: III MTTF at all states
sections.text: We focus on computing the signature of the subsystem obtained at each state 𝐱 \mathbf{x} in { 0 , 1 } n \{0,1\}^{n} , i.e., when restricting the system to the components that are working in state 𝐱 \mathbf{x} . Our main motivation for this, is the computation of the mean time-to-failure (MTTF) when the system is in any given state 𝐱 \mathbf{x} , and also derivation of repair policies based on these times. We will do this in the following setting for the joint probability distribution of the vector ( T 1 , … , T n ) (T_{1},\ldots,T_{n}) of failure times of components.

sections.heading: VII-A 3 Binomial failure rate and lethal-shock models
sections.text: In the binomial failure rate model [ 25 , 26 ] , which we denote by [BFR] and which originates in the multivariate exponential distribution of Marshall and Olkin [ 24 ] , each component fails on its own at rate λ ind \lambda_{\mathrm{ind}} , and common-cause shocks arrive at rate μ \mu and fail each working component independently with probability p p . In the lethal-shock model [ 26 ] , which we denote by [LSh], components fail on their own at rate λ ind \lambda_{\mathrm{ind}} , and lethal shocks arrive at rate ω \omega and fail all working components at once. Both are of Lévy-frailty Marshall-Olkin type, so ( 19 )–( 21 ) apply: [BFR] has Ψ ⁡ ( x ) = λ ind ​ x + μ ⁡ ( 1 − ( 1 − p ) x ) \Psi(x)=\lambda_{\mathrm{ind}}\,x+\mu\big(1-(1-p)^{x}\big) , a drift plus a compound Poisson subordinator with deterministic jumps of size log ⁡ ( 1 / ( 1 − p ) ) \log(1/(1-p)) , where a shock that fails no component leaves the survivor count unchanged [ 26 ] ; and [LSh] has Ψ ⁡ ( x ) = λ ind ​ x + ω \Psi(x)=\lambda_{\mathrm{ind}}\,x+\omega for x > 0 x>0 , a drift with killing at rate ω \omega . The Lévy-frailty class thus contains the standard common-cause models of probabilistic safety assessment.

sections.heading: VII-B Failure models used in the experiments
sections.text: In the experiments we use the Lévy-frailty Marshall-Olkin models above, for which the MTTF is monotone (Lemma 4 ): [Exp], and the six models [LFMO-C], [LFMO-G], [LFMO-IG], [LFMO-S], [BFR] and [LSh] with a common calibration. Models with single failures other than [Exp], such as sequential order statistics [ 19 ] and load-sharing models [ 18 ] , are not used, since they do not admit the calibration below and the MTTF of some of them is not monotone (Section V-A ). Every model is normalized so that Ψ ⁡ ( 1 ) = 1 \Psi(1)=1 ; since each component’s lifetime is exponentially distributed with rate Ψ ⁡ ( 1 ) \Psi(1) , one time unit is then the mean lifetime of a component, and all models differ only in how failures are grouped. For [LFMO-C] and [BFR] we take driftless compound Poisson subordinators, i.e., μ = 0 \mu=0 and λ ind = 0 \lambda_{\mathrm{ind}}=0 , respectively, so that, after the normalization, every model other than [Exp] has a single free parameter, which we fix through the pairwise beta factor.

The failure rate λ \lambda of each component of a redundant group is split as λ = λ ind + λ ccf \lambda=\lambda_{\mathrm{ind}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{ccf}} , into independent failures and common-cause events that fail the whole group, and the beta factor is the fraction λ ccf / λ \lambda_{\mathrm{ccf}}/\lambda . sections.heading: VII-C Systems used in the experiments
sections.text: We test our results on the 22 benchmark networks that Yeh et al. [ 13 ] use to compare algorithms for finding all minimal cuts, shown in Figure 3 . Each of them is a two-terminal network : a graph with a source s s and a terminal t t , whose edges are the components of the system and whose nodes do not fail. The system works iff s s and t t are connected by working edges, i.e., Φ ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) = 1 \Phi(\mathbf{x})=1 iff the edges i i with x i = 1 x_{i}=1 contain a path from s s to t t . This structure function is monotone, with Φ ⁡ ( 𝟎 ) = 0 \Phi(\mathbf{0})=0 and Φ ⁡ ( 𝟏 ) = 1 \Phi(\mathbf{1})=1 , and the minimal path sets are the edge sets of the simple paths from s s to t t . Hence the number n n of components of a system is its number of edges , not of nodes; it ranges from 5 5 to 30 30 , and 2 n 2^{n} from 32 32 to about 1.07 × 10 9 1.07\times 10^{9} . We use the edge lists of all 22 networks as they appear in Figure 7 of [ 13 ] , which leads to three features worth noting. First, networks 6 and 7 are drawn with arrows, and we read every edge of these two networks as an arc that can only be traversed in its direction. Network 6 then has four irrelevant components, the arcs leaving node 5, which cannot be reached from s s , so it is semi-coherent but not coherent; it has 13 13 minimal cuts, and network 7 has 110 110 , whereas, read as undirected graphs, they would have 26 26 and 133 133 , the value reported for network 7 in Table 9 of [ 13 ] . All other networks are undirected, and all their components are relevant. Second, network 21 is network 13 redrawn with the nodes renumbered, as noted in Section 6.3 of [ 13 ] : the two are isomorphic, with the terminals fixed, so they have the same signatures, MTTFs and policies, and we use network 21 only as a check of our computations (all its results coincide with those of network 13). sections.heading: VII-D Cost structure
sections.text: We use the cost structure ( 10 ) of Section V , with the cost of a system failure as the unit of cost, c sys = 1 c_{\mathrm{sys}}=1 . We parametrize the costs by ρ := n ​ c comp / c sys \rho:=nc_{\mathrm{comp}}/c_{\mathrm{sys}} , the cost of replacing all components relative to that of a system failure, and by σ := c set / c sys \sigma:=c_{\mathrm{set}}/c_{\mathrm{sys}} , the setup cost of a repair intervention, and we test ρ ∈ { 1 / 10 , 1 / 5 , 1 / 2 , 2 / 3 , 1 , 4 / 3 , 2 , 4 , 10 } \rho\in\{1/10,\,1/5,\,1/2,\,2/3,\,1,\,4/3,\,2,\,4,\,10\} and σ ∈ { 0 , 0.05 , 0.1 , 0.2 , 0.5 } \sigma\in\{0,\,0.05,\,0.1,\,0.2,\,0.5\} , i.e., 45 45 cost pairs. Values ρ < 1 \rho<1 describe safety- or production-critical systems, in which a system failure is more expensive than a complete renewal, and ρ > 1 \rho>1 systems whose components are expensive compared with the consequences of a failure.

sections.heading: VII-E Benchmark policies
sections.text: We compare the best MTTF-threshold policy, with cost v γ ∗ := min γ ⁡ L ​ T ​ M ​ C γ v^{\ast}_{\gamma}:=\min_{\gamma}LTMC^{\gamma} , with two benchmarks. The first are the r r -out-of- n n policies , which repair as soon as r r components have failed or the system has failed, for r = 1 , … , n r=1,\ldots,n [ 32 , 30 ] ; we write v r ∗ v^{\ast}_{r} for the cost of the best one. They only require counting failed components, and their cost follows from the signature of the complete system [ 30 ] . The one with r = n r=n , i.e., corrective maintenance, coincides with π γ \pi^{\gamma} for γ → 0 \gamma\to 0 , and, when all components are relevant, the one with r = 1 r=1 coincides with π 1 \pi^{1} . The second is the optimal state-based policy π ∗ \pi^{\ast} of Section V-B , with cost v state ∗ v^{\ast}_{\mathrm{state}} . Since the other policies are state-based, v state ∗ ≤ min ⁡ { v γ ∗ , v r ∗ } v^{\ast}_{\mathrm{state}}\leq\min\{v^{\ast}_{\gamma},v^{\ast}_{r}\} . By Section VI , every signature-threshold policy is also state-based, so the gap v γ ∗ / v state ∗ − 1 v^{\ast}_{\gamma}/v^{\ast}_{\mathrm{state}}-1 is an upper bound on the relative saving that any signature-threshold policy, whatever its weights, can achieve over the best MTTF-threshold policy.

sections.heading: Configurations
sections.text: A configuration consists of a system (22 networks of Figure 3 ) and a failure model (31 models of Section VII-B ), which gives 682 682 configurations, and 682 × 45 = 30,690 682\times 45=30{,}690 combinations of configuration and cost pair. For each system we run Algorithm 1 once, since it does not depend on the failure model, and store the classes of working states with the same counting vector, with their multiplicities. The same sweep also lists the minimal path sets (Section IV ); they are not needed for the policies, and we use them only to check the implementation, against an independent count of the simple s s – t t paths, and report their number in Table II . For each configuration we then compute, from the classes, the MTTF of all states, the whole curve γ ↦ ( T γ , N γ , P γ ) \gamma\mapsto(T^{\gamma},N^{\gamma},P^{\gamma}) at all its breakpoints (Proposition 3 ) and, for every cost pair, the best threshold and the best r r -out-of- n n policy. We compute the optimal state-based policy for the 19 systems with n ≤ 27 n\leq 27 , i.e., for all systems except the three with n = 30 n=30 , which gives 26,505 26{,}505 combinations.

sections.heading: Implementation
sections.text: All computations are implemented in Julia [ 41 ] and run sequentially, one system or configuration per core, on the high-performance computing cluster of Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez (nodes with two Intel Xeon E5-2650 processors at 2.0 GHz and 128 GB of RAM); all times below are measured on one core. Algorithm 1 stores each level as an integer matrix with one column per state, ordered lexicographically so that the column of each son is computed directly, and evaluates Φ \Phi by a reachability search on the working edges. The values Ψ ⁡ ( 1 ) , … , Ψ ⁡ ( n ) \Psi(1),\ldots,\Psi(n) and P w , w ′ P_{w,w^{\prime}} are computed in 512-bit arithmetic, since ( 20 ) is an alternating sum; the recursions given after Proposition 3 involve only nonnegative terms, so double precision suffices for the rest. Dinkelbach’s method is started at a value g 0 ≤ v γ ∗ g_{0}\leq v^{\ast}_{\gamma} and stops when h ⁡ ( 𝟏 ) ≥ − 10 − 12 ​ max ⁡ { 1 , c rep π k ​ ( 𝟏 ) } h(\mathbf{1})\geq-10^{-12}\max\{1,c^{\pi_{k}}_{\mathrm{rep}}(\mathbf{1})\} . The code, the experiment grid and the computed signatures are available at https://github.com/guidolagos/Subsystems .

sections.text: The number of distinct policies π γ \pi^{\gamma} , i.e., of breakpoints of γ ↦ L ​ T ​ M ​ C γ \gamma\mapsto LTMC^{\gamma} , ranges from 5 for the bridge (system 1) to about 1.3 1.3 million for systems 13 and 21 (Table II ). It varies little across the failure models of a system.

sections.heading: Shape of the cost curve
sections.text: The curve γ ↦ L ​ T ​ M ​ C γ \gamma\mapsto LTMC^{\gamma} is neither convex nor unimodal in general, i.e., the cost can increase and then decrease again as γ \gamma varies (Section V-A ). Among the 20,925 20{,}925 combinations of configuration and cost pair whose curve has at most 10,000 10{,}000 breakpoints, 74 % 74\% have a breakpoint whose cost exceeds the best cost on both of its sides, by more than 0.1 % 0.1\% in 48 % 48\% of them and by more than 1 % 1\% in 5.1 % 5.1\% , and by up to 5.3 % 5.3\% . Figure 4 shows two examples. As a consequence, simple search strategies may miss the best threshold: decreasing γ \gamma from 1 1 until the cost first increases loses more than 1 % 1\% with respect to the best threshold in 23 % 23\% of these combinations, more than 5 % 5\% in 9.7 % 9.7\% of them, and up to 62 % 62\% ; a grid of 201 equally spaced thresholds loses up to 2.9 % 2.9\% , and more than 1 % 1\% in 1.2 % 1.2\% of all 30,690 30{,}690 combinations. Evaluating all breakpoints, which Proposition 3 makes cheap, is therefore what guarantees the best threshold.

sections.heading: The best MTTF-threshold policy is near-optimal
sections.text: It is optimal, up to a relative error of 10 − 9 10^{-9} , in 17 % 17\% of the combinations, and its excess cost has a median of 0.36 % 0.36\% , a 90th percentile of 3.4 % 3.4\% and a 99th percentile of 13 % 13\% . The optimal state-based policy genuinely uses the identity of the failed components: in 95 % 95\% of the combinations there is at least one number of failed components at which it repairs at some, but not all, of the working states, and the median number of such levels is 6.

sections.heading: VII-J Computational effort of the policies
sections.text: Once the classes are stored, the whole curve γ ↦ ( T γ , N γ , P γ ) \gamma\mapsto(T^{\gamma},N^{\gamma},P^{\gamma}) of a failure model takes at most 2.8 2.8 seconds (Table II ), and the best threshold for a new cost pair is then found by evaluating ( 17 ) at every breakpoint, without recomputing anything else. The best r r -out-of- n n policy takes a fraction of a second. The optimal state-based policy, instead, needs a pass over the 2 n 2^{n} states for each iteration of Dinkelbach’s method and for each cost pair. Dinkelbach’s method converged in all 26,505 26{,}505 runs, with 2.4 2.4 passes on average and never more than five. One pass takes 0.8 0.8 seconds for n = 21 n=21 , 3.0 3.0 seconds for n = 23 n=23 and 52 52 seconds for n = 27 n=27 , so the optimal state-based policy for one cost pair takes a median of 197 197 seconds for system 17, and about 2.5 2.5 hours for the 45 cost pairs of one configuration, with a peak memory of 9.3 9.3 GB; extrapolating the n 2 ​ 2 n n^{2}2^{n} growth, it would take about a day per configuration and about 75 GB of memory for n = 30 n=30 , which is why we did not compute it for the three largest systems. This is the practical case for the MTTF-threshold policies: they come close to the optimal state-based policy at a small fraction of its cost, their cost curve serves every cost pair at once, and they are specified by a single number, the threshold γ \gamma , applied to an index, the MTTF, that is meaningful to practitioners.

sections.heading: VIII Conclusions and discussion
sections.text: We presented an algorithm that computes the structural signature and the MTTF of a monotone binary system at each of its 2 n 2^{n} states, with the same 2 n 2^{n} evaluations of the structure function needed for the signature of the complete system alone and a polynomial overhead in operations and memory, for exchangeable failure times whose survivor count is a continuous-time Markov chain, a setting that admits simultaneous failures. Under the Lévy-frailty Marshall-Olkin distribution, the monotonicity of the MTTF yields the long-run cost of every MTTF-threshold policy in a single pass over classes of states, and the per-state signature is a strictly finer decision criterion than the MTTF. On 22 benchmark networks with up to 30 components, the per-state computation took, for n = 30 n=30 , between 2.0 2.0 and 4.4 4.4 times as long as the enumeration for the signature of the complete system, and the best MTTF-threshold policy, tuned over all breakpoints of its cost curve, which is not unimodal, i.e., can increase and then decrease again as the threshold varies, was within a median of 0.36 % 0.36\% of the optimal state-based policy. This supports a simple rule for practitioners: monitor which components have failed, and repair when the MTTF of the current state falls below a fraction γ \gamma of that of a new system, with γ \gamma tuned exactly by our method. The rule is transparent and computed in seconds, whereas the optimal state-based policy costs 𝒪 ⁡ ( n 2 ​ 2 n ) \mathcal{O}(n^{2}2^{n}) operations per iteration and per cost setting. Our study has limitations that suggest further work. The algorithm enumerates the 2 n 2^{n} states, which limits it to a few dozen components; combining Lemma 1 with binary decision diagrams [ 14 ] may extend it to larger systems. The single-pass evaluation of the threshold policies relies on the monotonicity of the MTTF, which can fail for other models satisfying our assumptions, such as sequential order statistics in which the failure rate of the working components decreases as other components fail. Non-identical components, repair delays as in [ 42 ] , imperfect repairs and other families of systems are natural extensions. Finally, the gap between the best MTTF threshold and the optimal state-based policy, largest for nearly independent failures, cheap components and large systems, bounds what weighting the per-state signature differently can achieve; finding weights that close it, and comparing states with different numbers of failed components, remain open.
